doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Race in jazz and the DownBeat years
summary: Asked about race now, he recalls 1960s-70s resentment over union locals and studio jobs, Amiri Baraka's DownBeat column and Archie Shepp.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What about race, racial issues in jazz now?

Now — I think it’s pretty good now from what I can see. We went through some ups and downs. I was with DownBeat during a relatively interesting time as in the Chinese saying “may you live in interesting times.” There was a lot going on. You know there was a phenomenon which is very understandable and logical and was bound to happen sooner or later. In spite of the fact that jazz was one area where there were really good relations between the races, there was a residue of built-up and, you know, resentment among black musicians that they were unable to get the best jobs in the studios, that they were exposed to things like separate union locals where the scale for blacks was lower than for whites. You know that was an extraordinary circumstance. Local 802 in New York was never like that. That was always integrated. But even in a progressive city like Chicago you had two union locals and different scales. And, you know, many things like that. So that was kind of pent-up and it came out in the sixties and seventies in conjunction with all the civil rights activity then; the much more outspoken role that was taken on by blacks and it was bound to reflect itself in music too. So that, then you had some overtones of a little bit of strife there. And the magazine had inherited Amiri Baraka who was then still Leroi Jones, from Don DeMichael, who had very courageously engaged him as a columnist in spite of the publisher’s apprehension, and let him say what he wanted to say. And there was readers’ reaction from that and it was interesting, and it was something that was the right thing to do. So there was Archie Schepp, who was somewhat of a provocateur, and at the same time one of his best buddies and on-call instrumentalists was Roswell Rudd. So I mean what tended to be the case I’ve found is that there was a lot of talk but when you look behind the talk there really wasn’t that much of a change in what was going on.
